articles.title: AWS mumbles about its cost-busting networking tech when it should be shouting
articles.text: Last month I sat in a networking lab with AWS VP of Global Network Engineering Matt Rehder and cracked a joke about cage nuts cutting your hands to ribbons. I wasn't prepared for the blank stare I got in response, but I really should have been. Mind you, not because the joke wasn't funny (my jokes are hilarious), but rather because the world the joke was referencing no longer exists for them. Racks show up as assembled units, and apparently nobody screws hardware into anything in an AWS datacenter facility these days. It was a peek behind a curtain into a world that powers everything we do in cloud, but that remarkably few of us know exists. My Reg colleague Thomas Claburn toured the lab previously and gave us a deep dive into AWS's paper on this. In summary, "a flat, single-tier network wired in a deliberately near-random pattern leads to a way more resilient network that costs far less to run" and now you're up to speed. The part that I felt didn't get enough attention (and is why I invited myself to tour an AWS facility, much to AWS's surprise) is the economic part and how it impacts AWS customers. In short, their new networking approach can be up to 40 percent more energy efficient, and it's the default for most new datacenter builds (and dear reader, they are building a lot of those these days), and it's been completely invisible both inside and outside of the walls of the world's largest bookstore. The savings and cost efficiencies are real — so where do they go? Cost efficiencies abound  Seventeen years ago, Amazon SVP James Hamilton got on stage and pointed out [PDF] that network vendors ran businesses whose margins resembled those of mainframe vendors, who themselves in turn resembled starving pigs at a trough (colorful metaphor mine, but also... not wrong). His big issue with this distilled down to "they're in my way," and he plus his team set out to do something about it. It turns out that "what they did about it" was nothing less than rebuilding the entire networking stack themselves atop commodity hardware. This brings us to a few years ago. Their networking cost efficiencies were already far lower than they would have been running atop traditional networking vendors, and then their Resilient Network Graph shufflebox play took another axe to the cost of networking. So... where have those savings gone over these past few years? I asked point blank whether it was fair to say that they kept the margin improvement rather than passing it back to customers. Their answer was unequivocal: "From a cost perspective? Effectively, yes."  AWS cloud economics  It's easy to see that answer as damning, but I humbly suggest that if that's your reaction, you haven't been paying attention to broader industry trends these last few years. Unlike its competitors, AWS has not raised prices on existing SKUs. (Yes, the cost of GPU capacity blocks has been raised on a quarterly basis, but that's apparently how those were designed to work, much like a slow version of Spot Instances. And yes, they started charging per public IPv4 address a couple of years ago.) You can go out and spin up the same instance with 64GB of RAM that you could in 2020 and pay the same price today; that's not even increasing a price to keep up with inflation! And while there's a 9 percent increase to go from a Graviton4-based c8g.2xlarge to its equivalent c9g.2xlarge Graviton5 instance, nothing is making you upgrade. Frankly, given the component cost hikes, I'm more than a little astonished that they were able to hold the increase to 9 percent. Further, despite the madness-inducing level of granularity you see in an AWS bill with its millions of SKUs, it's worth noting that each SKU itself obscures dizzying levels of complexity. An EC2 instance charges you per hour (yes, it's metered by the second; do not email me), but that one charge covers the CPU, the RAM, the backplane, the power, the building's physical security, the IAM security bits that keep it from resembling a public computer/something from Microsoft Azure, the employees it takes to build and run these systems, and a stupendous amount of networking magic. A sea change in approach  One of those aspects of networking magic is that while it can be usuriously expensive to move traffic between Availability Zones (in major regions each gigabyte has a list price of a penny in and a penny out, so "two cents per gigabyte," which adds up), moving data inside of an AZ remains free. That's impressive when you start to realize how many different datacenter facilities can comprise a single AZ. It's damned impressive when you realize that AZs are expanding, data volumes are increasing, and that expansion comes with costs that thus far AWS has chosen to bear rather than pass on. It's significantly more expensive to move data out of AWS. Their now-defunct Snowball family of devices let you ship data back and forth to AWS. Sending one in cost a set fee, while sending one out cost that fee plus a per-GB charge. Annoying, right? That changed over the last year with the advent of AWS Interconnect - multicloud, which charges you nothing per GB, just an hourly port charge. There's a free tier of one 500 Mbps port per provider, which reduces to zero the AWS-side cost of sending that traffic to GCP, Oracle, and soon Azure. For comparison's sake, it'd be roughly $12,000 to send a month's saturation of that port across the open internet. Stated more plainly, this has never been done before on the AWS side, and it's fascinating. While it's not the primary area of focus for the folks I talked to, I nonetheless asked them about it for an on-the-record answer: "We know customers do not like rate-based network charges because it’s hard to predict their cost, which is why we are moving towards flat-rate pricing for new network products." Well slap me naked and hide my clothes; I'd be less surprised if Matt Garman gave his next re:Invent keynote in iambic pentameter. This bears watching; it's more interesting to me that it comes at a time when prices are rising instead of falling. How hard can it be? Very hard The problem is that a lot of what AWS does is invisible. For example, why am I telling you this instead of AWS? AWS concedes that they're generally bad at telling their own story, but they clearly want to tell it. Historically, they've punted to customers to tell their own stories, on the belief that the benefit will accrue to them. Here's my favorite example: the hard part of a near-random network isn't the cabling so much as the routing. Every protocol you've heard of (BGP, OSPF, a few Cisco-specific protocols that nobody sane uses, etc.) computes shortest paths, and "shortest path" stops meaning much when there are roughly thousands of equivalent routes between any two points. AWS solved that with a protocol called SIDR (Scalable Intent-Driven Routing, pronounced "cider," like the CIDR method for allocating IP addresses because these people are malevolent at naming things) that runs the control plane, while Spraypoint picks up the actual forwarding path. They presented SIDR publicly at re:Invent in 2023, then covered it again at the "Monday Night Live" re:Invent keynote in 2024. Then they published the RNG paper, which doesn't mention SIDR at all. As best I can tell, nobody outside the company has ever connected the protocol to the network it makes possible. I had to ask just in case I was missing something. I'm right. It isn't a secret! They just never got around to mentioning how important it was to making the whole thing go. Unfortunately, their lack of storytelling prowess about these things isn't working for them. The perception runs the other way: the market believes that the neoclouds and the Nvidia reference designs are better. They aren't. You can build a neocloud without knowing much about networking, and some outfits clearly have. A lot of datacenter networks are run by absolute clowns. I know this; I used to be one of said clowns before I got religion / discovered I could pay a cloud provider to make this stuff Matt Rehder's problem. AWS has gotten so good at making network arcana invisible that we don't really stop and think about just how wild it is that you can get damned near full line-rate between any two points in AWS and it just works. In the datacenters you or I build, you get to worry about fun things like "the switch at the top of the rack can only push so much traffic, so not every node can talk at full speed all the time." I have never encountered a real-world scenario of that being a concern in AWS. As a result, when folks set out to build their own datacenters, they don't know what they don't know after a generation of that complexity being hidden away from them, and they approach it with a sense of "how hard could it be?" It is extremely hard, and I have little confidence that the neoclouds spinning up new DC facilities overnight are paying attention to this. I asked Rehder directly whether the "ML datacenter facilities" AWS was launching in places like Mississippi were taking shortcuts since GPU workloads might have different requirements. He looked at me as if I were nuts; every datacenter they build is to the same spec. But customers won't care about that until right after they really should have cared about that; I have faith that a datacenter failure will be sufficiently public, embarrassing, and impactful so as to remind them. The tree of uptime must be periodically refreshed with the blood of massive outages. The humble mumble The folks I spoke to at AWS about this have built something that most of their own customers will never know exists, and they seem generally untroubled by that fact. I found that more admirable than I would have expected to; it's the very definition of thankless work, and AWS shines here. The reason the work is invisible is simply because it succeeds. And they're so humble about it! They politely chuckled at my joke about cage nuts once they got the reference, and I politely chuckled at their joke about how each year's switch is painted the Pantone "Color of the Year," which it turns out was in fact not even slightly a joke. AWS gets a lot wrong. They have ridiculous marketing campaigns, they build five services that do mostly the same thing and then name them like malevolent toddlers, and they've never found a partner they couldn't find a way to compete with. But when it comes to the "chop wood, carry water" type of work that makes the entire cloud possible, the kind that would put most of a keynote audience to sleep, they're the finest in the world. They're just bad at telling the world about it. ®

articles.title: Rolls-Royce Offers India Sovereign Assurance on AMCA Engine With 100% ToT, Sources Say
articles.text:
Rolls-Royce is offering India strong government-to-government backing for its proposed fighter engine programme, with sources telling idrw.org that the British company wants its commitments on technology transfer and indigenous development to be supported at the sovereign level.
According to sources, the proposed G2G framework would provide India with sovereign assurance that the engine programme would not be abruptly scrapped, delayed or restricted in the future, particularly when it comes to technology transfer. This is seen as an important safeguard for India as the country looks to develop an indigenous fighter-engine capability.
Rolls-Royce has offered 100 percent technology transfer to India as part of its proposal for the next-generation fighter engine. The company has also indicated that the entire engine would be developed in India, rather than limiting Indian participation to assembly or licensed production.
The approach is significant because India is seeking much greater control over fighter-engine technology. Complete domestic development could allow Indian engineers to understand, modify and upgrade the engine without remaining dependent on foreign approvals for every major change.
The Rolls-Royce proposal has gained additional significance following the company’s partnership with Reliance Industries (RIL). The two companies recently announced plans to establish a joint venture focused on aerospace and gas-turbine technologies in India.
According to information previously reported by idrw.org, Rolls-Royce has also been offering a core architecture that could be developed in different thrust classes. The proposed engine core could initially generate around 73 kN and 88 kN of dry thrust, providing a technological foundation for more powerful future variants.
The long-term objective could be to develop afterburning engines in the 120 kN and 145 kN thrust classes using the same basic technology architecture. Such engines could potentially power future versions of the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) or even its successor aircraft.
This upgrade path is arguably as important as the initial AMCA engine requirement. Instead of India receiving a fixed foreign engine that eventually reaches its development limit, a scalable architecture could allow Indian industry to progressively increase thrust and improve the engine’s performance as materials, turbine technology and manufacturing capabilities advance.
The proposed sovereign backing is intended to address another concern: technology transfer cannot be allowed to become vulnerable to future geopolitical pressure.
For India, the attraction of the Rolls-Royce offer therefore goes beyond obtaining an engine for AMCA. If the proposed arrangements are finalised as described by sources, India could gain access to an engine development ecosystem that includes technology transfer, domestic manufacturing and the ability to pursue future upgrades.
The immediate requirement remains the development of a suitable powerplant for AMCA, but the larger strategic objective is clear: India wants to build the ability to design and develop increasingly powerful fighter engines within the country.

articles.title: D-Propulse Eyes 10 kN RDE Engine: A Thrust Class With Applications From Micro launchers to Intergalactic landers
articles.text:
D-Propulse founder and CEO Saurav Jha, speaking on the 50th episode of the Ctrl Alt Defence podcast, revealed that the company’s already-validated 5 kN Rotating Detonation Engine could scale to 7 kN without significant design changes, and expressed confidence that a 10 kN RDE is achievable within the next few years. While Jha stopped short of naming a specific end application for the larger engine, the 10 kN thrust class sits squarely in what aerospace engineers consider a genuine sweet spot, too small for primary heavy-lift boosters, but ideally suited to a surprisingly wide range of advanced space, missile, and unmanned aircraft applications.
From 5 kN to 7 kN: An Easier Near-Term Step
The relatively modest engineering lift required to push from 5 kN to 7 kN reflects genuine underlying momentum in D-Propulse’s combustor design. The company’s current engine, already validated at Technology Readiness Level 5 following a sustained hot-fire test at a DRDO facility in Hyderabad, integrates an aerospike nozzle specifically chosen to maintain propulsion efficiency across a wide altitude envelope. According to the company’s own reported test data, its newer combustor designs have already demonstrated efficiency gains exceeding 35 percent alongside a threefold increase in thrust compared to earlier configurations, evidence that the underlying architecture has real scaling headroom built in rather than being pushed to its physical limits at 5 kN.
Why 10 kN Is Considered a Genuine Sweet Spot
Even without a confirmed target application, the 10 kN thrust class carries real significance across several distinct aerospace domains, each shaped by a common thread: RDE propulsion’s pressure-gain combustion advantage translates directly into more range, payload, or speed for a given engine size and fuel load.
Upper-stage space manoeuvring and orbital insertion represents one plausible avenue. A 10 kN RDE running on propellant combinations like liquid oxygen paired with methane or hydrogen could serve as primary propulsion for small-lift orbital launch vehicles designed to deploy Low Earth Orbit constellations, an increasingly crowded and commercially important segment of the global space industry. The same thrust class could function as a high-efficiency kick stage for medium-lift rockets, where detonation-based pressure recovery’s specific impulse gains would let a stage either carry heavier payloads or burn meaningfully less propellant during orbital transfer and deep-space trajectory correction manoeuvres. Lunar or planetary landers represent a further natural fit, since descent and ascent stages demand high reliability and strong thrust-to-weight performance from a minimal footprint, exactly the kind of profile a throttleable rotating detonation rocket engine could deliver, freeing up mass budget for scientific payload rather than propulsion hardware.
Hypersonic missiles and high-speed boosters form a second major application cluster. A 10 kN class RDE is well suited to powering the boost phase of tactical or strategic hypersonic glide vehicles, where the technology’s ability to release massive energy within a radically compact volume keeps the overall missile body smaller, freeing internal space for guidance electronics and warhead payload instead of bulkier conventional propulsion. This thrust class also aligns with how major defence research organisations internationally, including DARPA and the US Air Force Research Laboratory, have approached lower-to-mid tier RDEs as components within Turbine-Based or Rocket-Based Combined Cycle engines, using detonation propulsion to violently accelerate a vehicle through the difficult transonic barrier up to speeds where ramjet or scramjet propulsion can take over.
Tactical long-range standoff missiles represent a third plausible destination. Heavy air-to-ground or anti-ship missiles requiring sustained high-supersonic speed over extended range could benefit substantially from a 10 kN-class detonation engine, where the fuel efficiency gains translate directly into either extended combat range or a heavier, more effective warhead without growing the missile’s overall dimensions, an important constraint given limited launcher cell space on aircraft and naval vessels alike.
Advanced drone and unmanned combat aerial vehicle propulsion rounds out the likely application set. High-speed expendable UCAVs, whether built for swarming tactics or high-speed reconnaissance in contested airspace, could use compact detonation-based powerplants to achieve sprint speeds that conventional turbojets or small turbofans simply can’t match within an equivalent weight budget, a genuinely important consideration for expendable or semi-expendable unmanned platforms where cost and mass constraints are especially tight.
Where This Fits D-Propulse’s Broader Strategic Vision
Jha has been consistently vocal about viewing RDE technology as something considerably broader than a single-product venture. He has described the technology as a general-purpose capability comparable in long-term significance to artificial intelligence or electricity, one he expects to eventually permeate both civilian and military aviation, rockets, and cruise missiles alike. That framing helps explain why D-Propulse hasn’t necessarily locked itself into a single target application for a future 10 kN engine, the company’s stated approach is to build a broader stack of RDE-based propulsion solutions applicable across drones, missiles, and other high-speed platforms, rather than engineering narrowly toward one specific end use from the outset.
A Realistic Note on the Distance Still Ahead
It’s worth grounding this ambition against where D-Propulse actually stands today. What the company has demonstrated so far are ground tests of a relatively small-scale prototype; the gap between a combustor proven on a test rig and a fully flight-cleared, operationally deployed engine remains substantial, and that gap doesn’t shrink simply because a larger thrust class is targeted. D-Propulse’s own publicly stated roadmap reflects this reality, targeting a flight-ready 5 kN-class system by December 2027 and offering RDE-powered munitions for Indian military user trials only by December 2029. A 10 kN engine, even if development proves achievable within a few years as Jha suggests, would still need to pass through comparable validation stages before reaching any of the applications outlined above.
The Bottom Line
A 10 kN Rotating Detonation Engine wouldn’t need a single killer application to be strategically significant, its real value lies in sitting at a thrust level relevant to microlauncher upper stages, planetary landers, hypersonic boost-glide systems, tactical standoff missiles, and high-speed unmanned platforms simultaneously. That versatility is precisely why Jha’s confidence in reaching this thrust class within a few years matters beyond any single programme, it would give India’s fledgling private RDE industry a genuinely flexible building block applicable across space, missile, and drone propulsion domains that have historically required entirely separate engine development efforts.

articles.text:
India has taken its first formal step toward the Global Combat Air Programme, the trilateral sixth-generation fighter jet effort led by the United Kingdom, Japan, and Italy, joining as a “dialogue partner.” The development was first reported by Tribune News Service, which cited UK officials confirming that India and the UK had held detailed discussions on the matter, with New Delhi nominated for the status as the two sides explored deeper engagement on the programme popularly known as Tempest.
India’s entry into the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) as a dialogue partner gives New Delhi a formal channel to engage with the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan on their next-generation combat aircraft programme. However, the status should not be confused with full membership — or with the more closely defined observer role.
The distinction is important because GCAP is already a major fighter-development programme involving the UK, Japan and Italy, with the three countries working towards a next-generation combat aircraft expected to enter service around 2035.
What does dialogue partner mean?
For India, dialogue partner is primarily a political and strategic engagement mechanism.It allows New Delhi to participate in high-level discussions with the three GCAP countries covering broader security requirements, future combat-air capabilities, industrial cooperation and possible areas of technological collaboration.
Crucially, India does not become a formal GCAP development partner simply by acquiring dialogue-partner status. It does not automatically assume the financial, industrial or operational commitments associated with the programme.
The arrangement therefore gives India room to explore cooperation while keeping its options open.This is particularly relevant because India is developing its own Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA). New Delhi can continue with AMCA while maintaining a formal dialogue with countries developing one of the world’s most advanced future fighter programmes.
How is an observer different?
An official observer has a more structured relationship with the programme itself. Canada, for example, became GCAP’s first observer in 2026. Its observer arrangement gives it greater insight into the programme’s governance, capabilities, industrial structure and security requirements. This allows Canada to assess the programme more closely and examine whether deeper participation could make sense in the future.
An observer therefore has greater emphasis on monitoring and evaluating the programme, whereas a dialogue partner is primarily involved in strategic and political discussions.
The distinction can be simplified:
- Dialogue Partner: Strategic and political engagement.
- Official Observer: Closer monitoring and evaluation of the programme.
- Full Partner: Formal participation in development, funding, industrial work and programme governance.
Why India’s status matters
India’s dialogue-partner position could eventually become useful if New Delhi identifies areas where cooperation with GCAP countries complements its own aerospace programmes.
The most obvious areas could include advanced avionics, sensors, electronic warfare, propulsion, weapons and other technologies relevant to future combat aircraft. However, dialogue-partner status itself should not be interpreted as giving India access to classified GCAP technology or design information.
For New Delhi, the biggest advantage may actually be strategic flexibility.
India can engage closely with the UK, Japan and Italy and understand where sixth-generation combat aviation is heading without immediately committing itself to another multinational fighter-development programme.

articles.title: Tejas Mk1A’s Uttam GaN AESA Radar Could Give Later Production Jets a Major Edge Over Earlier EL/M-2052 Equipped Fleet
articles.text:
The Indian Air Force’s Tejas Mk1A programme is set to witness a significant technological evolution as later production batches transition from the Israeli EL/M-2052 Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar to the indigenous Uttam AESA radar developed by DRDO’s Electronics and Radar Development Establishment (LRDE). While both radars belong to the AESA family and offer modern multi-mode capabilities, the change is more than simply replacing one sensor with another. It represents a shift from mature Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) semiconductor technology to next-generation Gallium Nitride (GaN), bringing improvements in power efficiency, thermal performance, electronic warfare resilience, and long-term indigenous control.
The first contract for 83 Tejas Mk1A aircraft is expected to feature the EL/M-2052 radar, while follow-on production batches, including the planned procurement of an additional 97 aircraft, are expected to increasingly incorporate the Uttam GaN AESA radar. If implemented as planned, the transition would create two distinct capability standards within the Tejas Mk1A fleet, with the later aircraft benefiting from advances in semiconductor technology and complete indigenous software ownership.
GaAs vs GaN: The Technology Behind the Upgrade
The principal distinction between the EL/M-2052 and Uttam lies in the semiconductor material used in their transmit/receive (T/R) modules. The EL/M-2052 employs Gallium Arsenide (GaAs), a well-established technology that has powered many modern AESA radars around the world. GaAs offers excellent reliability and has been proven in operational service across multiple fighter aircraft. However, it has physical limitations in terms of power density, thermal tolerance, and electrical efficiency.
The Uttam radar, by contrast, is expected to adopt Gallium Nitride (GaN) technology for future production. GaN is considered the next generation of radar semiconductor material because it can operate at significantly higher voltages and temperatures while delivering substantially greater power output.
Compared with GaAs, GaN transmit/receive modules can produce considerably more radio frequency energy while consuming less electrical power. Their higher thermal tolerance also reduces the likelihood of performance degradation during prolonged high-power operation, enabling the radar to sustain demanding combat modes for longer durations.
These characteristics have made GaN the preferred technology for many of the world’s newest fighter radars, naval radars, and integrated air defence systems.
Detection Performance Could Improve Noticeably
Radar detection range depends on numerous variables, including target radar cross-section, operating frequency, atmospheric conditions, and processing algorithms. Nevertheless, improvements in transmitter efficiency directly influence overall radar performance.
The EL/M-2052 is generally assessed to provide detection ranges in the region of 150 to 200 kilometres against fighter-sized targets with a radar cross-section of approximately one square metre under favourable conditions. A GaN-equipped Uttam radar is expected to improve effective detection performance through higher transmitted power and better receiver sensitivity. While exact figures remain classified, defence analysts estimate that GaN technology could provide an increase of approximately 20 to 25 percent in effective detection range compared to equivalent GaAs systems.
Equally important, the higher effective radiated power enhances the radar’s ability to maintain target tracks under challenging electromagnetic conditions, particularly when operating against electronic countermeasures.
Improved Thermal Management Enables Sustained Performance
One of GaN’s greatest operational advantages lies in thermal management. Every radar converts electrical energy into radio frequency energy, but a significant portion inevitably becomes heat. Excessive temperatures reduce component lifespan and may force the radar to limit output power to protect sensitive electronics.
GaAs systems typically require more intensive cooling and can approach thermal limits sooner during extended high-power operation. GaN devices, by comparison, tolerate substantially higher operating temperatures without compromising reliability. This enables the radar to operate at elevated power settings for longer periods while reducing thermal stress on internal components.
For combat aircraft operating extended air patrols or multiple intercept missions during high-intensity operations, this translates into greater operational endurance and potentially lower maintenance demands.
Enhanced Electronic Warfare Resilience
Modern aerial combat increasingly depends on success within the electromagnetic spectrum. Electronic attack systems attempt to degrade radar performance through noise jamming, deceptive techniques, and false target generation. Consequently, radar performance can no longer be measured solely by maximum detection range.
The higher power output available from GaN technology improves the radar’s effective radiated power, increasing its ability to overcome electronic interference. This enhances burn-through performance—the point at which genuine target echoes become distinguishable from hostile jamming.
In contested airspace, stronger transmitted signals can improve target tracking reliability and help maintain radar performance despite sophisticated electronic countermeasures. However, it is important to note that overall electronic warfare effectiveness depends on multiple factors beyond transmitter power alone, including waveform design, signal processing, adaptive algorithms, antenna performance, and the capabilities of the opposing jammer.
Greater Integration with Indigenous Weapons
Another major advantage of the Uttam radar lies in software sovereignty. As an indigenous development, Uttam can be fully integrated with Indian-developed weapon systems without dependence on foreign intellectual property restrictions.
Future integration with weapons such as the Astra Mk1, Astra Mk2, the SFDR-powered Astra Mk3 (Gandiva), and the Rudram anti-radiation missile family can be undertaken directly by Indian agencies, allowing software modifications to be implemented more rapidly.
This flexibility extends beyond missile integration to future upgrades involving artificial intelligence-assisted target management, advanced electronic warfare techniques, and cooperative engagement capabilities. By contrast, imported radar systems generally involve varying degrees of proprietary software protection, meaning certain modifications may require cooperation from the original manufacturer depending on contractual arrangements.
Supporting India’s Unified Electronic Warfare Architecture
The Tejas Mk1A incorporates an advanced electronic warfare suite designed to improve survivability in contested environments. The indigenous Uttam radar is expected to integrate closely with this architecture, enabling faster data exchange between the radar, electronic support measures, self-protection jammer, mission computer, and onboard sensors.
Such integration can improve overall situational awareness by allowing sensor information to be processed and distributed more efficiently across the aircraft’s mission systems. The result is not merely a more capable radar, but a more integrated combat platform capable of making better use of all available onboard sensors.
Logistics and Wartime Sustainability
Perhaps the greatest long-term benefit of adopting Uttam lies outside technical performance. An indigenous radar significantly reduces dependence on overseas suppliers for future upgrades, software enhancements, spare parts, and lifecycle support.
During peacetime, this provides greater flexibility for incremental capability improvements. During wartime or periods of geopolitical tension, domestic control over production, maintenance, and software development reduces vulnerability to supply chain disruptions or export restrictions.
DRDO and HAL would possess the ability to develop mission-specific software enhancements, introduce new electronic warfare modes, and integrate future indigenous weapons without relying on external approval processes. This level of technological sovereignty is increasingly viewed as a strategic advantage as nations seek to reduce dependence on foreign defence technologies.
Two Generations Within the Same Fleet
As production progresses, the Tejas Mk1A fleet may effectively consist of two technological standards. The earlier aircraft equipped with the EL/M-2052 will continue to field a highly capable, combat-proven AESA radar offering excellent multi-target tracking, air-to-air and air-to-ground modes, and reliable operational performance.
The later batches equipped with Uttam are expected to build upon that foundation by leveraging GaN technology, improved power efficiency, stronger electronic warfare resilience, deeper integration with indigenous weapons, and complete domestic control over future upgrades. While both radar systems are capable modern AESA designs, the shift to GaN represents a natural technological progression similar to trends seen in leading aerospace industries worldwide.

articles.title: Can India Integrate BrahMos-NG on Rafale Without French Source Code? The Technical Challenges and Possible Workarounds
articles.text:
The possibility of integrating India’s upcoming BrahMos-NG supersonic cruise missile onto the Dassault Rafale has generated considerable interest. While the combination would significantly enhance the Indian Air Force’s stand-off strike capability, the integration process is far more complex than simply mounting a missile beneath the aircraft.
Industry experts point out that integrating any new weapon onto a modern Western fighter requires access to the aircraft’s Interface Control Document (ICD) and, in many cases, software support from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM). Without cooperation from Dassault Aviation, achieving full native integration would be extremely challenging.
Why the Interface Control Document Matters
Modern combat aircraft rely on tightly integrated digital avionics. The aircraft’s mission computer communicates with every external store through predefined electrical interfaces and software protocols.
The ICD specifies how information such as weapon status, targeting coordinates, health monitoring, power supply and launch commands are exchanged between the aircraft and the weapon. Without this information, the aircraft cannot safely recognise, configure or release a new missile through its existing avionics architecture.
In addition, Western fighters incorporate multiple software-controlled safety interlocks to ensure weapons can only be armed and released under approved flight conditions. These protections are deeply embedded within the aircraft’s mission systems.
Potential Alternative Integration Approaches
Should OEM support not be available, engineers could theoretically explore alternative integration methods that minimise modifications to the aircraft’s core mission computer. One possible approach involves developing a standalone Weapon Management Unit (WMU) or a smart pylon. In this architecture, the external hardware would manage communications with the missile independently of the Rafale’s primary avionics.
Rather than requiring deep integration into the aircraft’s mission software, the smart pylon could perform many of the weapon-management functions itself while receiving only limited inputs from the aircraft. Dedicated cockpit controls or independent display interfaces could then allow the pilot to manage the missile without extensive modifications to the Rafale’s operational flight software.
Another theoretical method would involve extensive Hardware-in-the-Loop (HWIL) testing. Engineers could build sophisticated ground-based integration laboratories that replicate the aircraft’s electrical interfaces, allowing them to validate launcher behaviour, electrical compatibility and weapon responses before flight testing. Such simulation facilities are already widely used during the development of complex aerospace systems to reduce technical risk before airborne trials.
Reverse Engineering Faces Significant Barriers
Another frequently discussed concept is analysing communications between existing weapons and the aircraft to understand the underlying interface.
However, modern fourth- and fifth-generation Western fighters employ encrypted digital communications, authentication protocols and secure avionics architectures designed specifically to prevent unauthorised integration. Even if basic electrical signalling could be characterised, reproducing the complete software environment required for operational certification would remain an extremely difficult undertaking.
Certification Remains the Biggest Challenge
Even if engineers successfully established technical communication between the aircraft and a new missile, achieving operational clearance would present another major hurdle.
Any weapon integrated onto a frontline fighter must undergo extensive certification covering structural loads, aerodynamic behaviour, flutter characteristics, electromagnetic compatibility, aircraft controllability, safe separation during release, software validation and live firing trials. For a large, high-speed stand-off weapon such as BrahMos-NG, these certification activities would require extensive flight-test campaigns before the system could be declared operational.
Strategic Considerations
India has steadily increased its indigenous weapon integration capabilities over the past two decades, successfully integrating weapons such as the Astra family of beyond-visual-range missiles, Rudram anti-radiation missiles and numerous precision-guided munitions across indigenous aircraft.
However, integrating indigenous weapons onto foreign-origin platforms generally remains easier when undertaken with OEM cooperation, as this reduces technical complexity, certification timelines and programme risk. For this reason, most defence analysts believe that formal collaboration with Dassault Aviation would remain the most practical and lowest-risk path if BrahMos-NG were ever selected for integration on the Rafale.

articles.title: IAF Fighter Crisis: Why Mass-Inducting CATS Warrior and Ghatak UCAVs Could Be a Faster Solution
articles.text:
The Indian Air Force’s long-standing shortage of combat squadrons is becoming increasingly difficult to solve through fighter procurement alone. Fighters remain the most important component of any modern air force, and India will continue to need large numbers of manned combat aircraft. However, the reality is that the IAF is unlikely to reach its desired force level of around 42 fighter squadrons in the near term. This creates a capability gap that needs to be addressed through additional means.
One potential solution is a much more aggressive push toward mass induction of unmanned combat aircraft, particularly platforms such as HAL’s CATS Warrior and the DRDO Ghatak programme. Rather than viewing these UCAVs as replacements for fighters, India could use them as force multipliers that supplement manned aircraft and provide additional combat mass much faster than a conventional fighter-production programme could achieve.
The fundamental problem is numbers. India’s fighter fleet is currently transitioning between generations, with older aircraft such as the MiG-21 already retired and other legacy platforms gradually approaching the end of their useful service lives. At the same time, the Tejas Mk1A programme is still ramping up, the Tejas Mk2 remains under development and AMCA is years away from becoming available in meaningful numbers.
Even if these programmes proceed successfully, replacing ageing fighters and simultaneously expanding the fleet to the desired squadron strength will require considerable time. Aircraft production is constrained not only by final assembly but also by engines, radar systems, electronic warfare equipment, weapons, trained pilots, maintenance infrastructure and supply chains.
This is where UCAVs could provide an alternative path to increasing combat mass.
A platform such as CATS Warrior is conceptually different from a conventional fighter. It is intended to operate alongside manned aircraft and can potentially undertake high-risk missions without placing a pilot inside the aircraft. Depending on its final configuration, such a system could conduct surveillance, electronic warfare, suppression of enemy air defences and strike missions while accompanying manned fighters.
The Ghatak programme represents an even more ambitious Indian effort to develop an autonomous stealth-oriented combat aircraft. Its eventual operational capability could provide the IAF with a platform capable of penetrating contested airspace and attacking high-value targets while reducing the risk to human pilots.
The major advantage of UCAVs in the present situation is therefore not that they are better than fighters. They are not. Their advantage is that they could potentially be produced and deployed in large numbers without the enormous human-resource burden associated with manned combat aviation.
Every additional fighter squadron requires pilots, instructors, ground crews and extensive training pipelines. An unmanned combat fleet would still require highly trained operators, maintenance personnel and mission planners, but the manpower model could be fundamentally different.
This opens the possibility of a mass rather than squadron-based approach to augmenting the IAF. Instead of waiting for dozens of additional manned fighter squadrons, India could progressively build large numbers of autonomous and optionally networked combat aircraft that operate alongside existing fighters.
The concept becomes particularly relevant in a two-front scenario. The IAF must maintain the ability to respond simultaneously to threats from both the western and northern fronts. Concentrating the majority of India’s most capable manned fighters in one theatre inevitably creates risk elsewhere.
UCAVs could provide additional persistence and weapons capacity without requiring India to maintain an equivalent number of pilots. A formation consisting of a manned fighter accompanied by several unmanned combat aircraft could potentially generate more sensors, electronic warfare capacity and weapons than the fighter could carry independently.
The concept also changes the economics of attrition. In a major conflict, expensive frontline fighters may become increasingly difficult to replace. If a lower-cost unmanned platform can perform selected strike, reconnaissance or suppression missions, commanders could potentially accept a higher level of UCAV attrition while preserving scarce manned aircraft.
However, this does not mean India should abandon fighter acquisition. Quite the opposite is true. Tejas Mk1A, Tejas Mk2, Rafale, Su-30MKI upgrades and AMCA remain essential components of the future IAF. UCAVs cannot fully replicate the flexibility, situational awareness and decision-making capability of a human pilot, particularly in complex air-to-air engagements.
The most sensible approach would therefore be a manned-unmanned force structure. Fighters would remain the core combat platform, while UCAVs would extend their reach and increase the number of combat assets available to commanders.
For this concept to work, however, India would need to accelerate autonomous mission management, secure datalinks, artificial intelligence, sensor fusion, electronic warfare and human-machine teaming. UCAVs cannot simply be remotely controlled aircraft if they are expected to operate in heavily contested environments where communications may be degraded or denied.
This is where programmes such as CATS Warrior and Ghatak become strategically important. They provide India with an opportunity to develop the technologies required for a future air force in which a single pilot could potentially control or coordinate multiple unmanned platforms.
The IAF’s fighter shortage is unlikely to disappear quickly. Waiting for the fleet to reach the desired squadron strength before addressing the capability gap would leave India exposed during the transition period. A larger UCAV force could provide an additional layer of combat power while the manned fighter fleet gradually expands.
The central argument is therefore not fighters versus UCAVs. It is fighters plus UCAVs.
Fighters will remain the backbone of India’s combat aviation for decades. But if India accepts that reaching the required number of manned fighter squadrons will take time, then mass deployment of systems such as CATS Warrior and eventually Ghatak could provide a practical way to increase combat mass much sooner.

articles.title: Pakistan Unveils 3,000 km-Range Delta Wing D-248 Loitering Munition: Shahed Clone Raises Questions Over Possible Chinese Technology Links
articles.text:
Pakistan has publicly showcased a new long-range unmanned aerial system (UAS) called the Delta Wing Loitering Munition (D-248), claiming it offers an operational range of up to 3,000 kilometres and endurance of 12–14 hours. Displayed by Heavy Industries Taxila (HIT), the drone immediately attracted attention because its claimed range exceeds that of nearly every missile currently fielded by Pakistan, prompting questions about its technological origins and the feasibility of the published specifications.
The aircraft’s external appearance bears a striking resemblance to Iran’s Shahed family of long-range loitering munitions, while several design elements also resemble Chinese unmanned systems. Although Pakistan has not disclosed the propulsion system, guidance package, or operational status of the platform, the D-248 could represent Islamabad’s attempt to enter the growing market for long-range one-way attack drones capable of conducting strategic strikes deep inside enemy territory.
A Shahed-Style Delta Wing Design with Ambitious Performance Claims
According to the specifications displayed alongside the aircraft, the D-248 is a delta-wing loitering munition with a maximum take-off weight (MTOW) of approximately 240 kg and a payload capacity between 30 and 50 kg. The brochure claims the platform has a wingspan of 3.3 metres, can operate at altitudes up to 4,500 metres, cruises at around 185 km/h, and reaches a maximum speed of 225 km/h. The most eye-catching figures, however, are its 2,200–3,000 km operational range and 12 to 14 hours of endurance.
If accurate, these numbers would place the D-248 among the longest-range loitering munitions currently known, approaching the endurance and reach normally associated with much larger unmanned aircraft rather than tactical one-way attack drones.
Visually, the drone features a triangular delta wing, compact fuselage, rear-mounted control surfaces, and what appears to be a pusher-propeller configuration concealed behind the airframe. This aerodynamic layout closely resembles Iran’s Shahed-136 series, which has become one of the world’s most recognised loitering munitions following its extensive operational use in recent conflicts.
Claimed Range Exceeds Most Pakistani Missile Systems
Perhaps the most remarkable aspect of the D-248 is its advertised range. Pakistan’s current missile inventory includes systems such as the Babur land-attack cruise missile and the Shaheen family of ballistic missiles. While some strategic ballistic missiles possess greater reach, among conventionally employed precision strike systems the claimed 3,000 km range of the D-248 would place it beyond the operational reach of most cruise missiles in Pakistan’s inventory.
Such a range would theoretically allow launches from deep inside Pakistani territory while threatening targets far beyond South Asia. Combined with a relatively low radar signature and slow speed typical of loitering munitions, such a platform could complicate air defence planning by forcing defenders to monitor threats over extended periods.
However, the published specifications also raise technical questions. Achieving a 3,000 km range with a 240 kg aircraft carrying a 30–50 kg payload requires exceptional fuel efficiency, lightweight composite construction, and an engine capable of operating continuously for more than half a day. Without details regarding propulsion, fuel capacity, navigation systems, or flight profile, independent verification of these claims remains impossible.
Design Strongly Echoes the Iranian Shahed Family
The D-248’s external configuration immediately invites comparisons with the Iranian Shahed series. The triangular wing planform, compact fuselage, simple aerodynamic design, and apparent emphasis on low-cost mass production all mirror concepts successfully employed by Iran. The Shahed family demonstrated that relatively inexpensive loitering munitions could overwhelm sophisticated air defence networks through saturation attacks.
Pakistan has maintained defence cooperation with several countries over the years, making the possibility of technology transfer or design inspiration difficult to dismiss. While there is no public evidence confirming direct Iranian involvement in the D-248 programme, the similarities are significant enough to generate speculation within defence circles.
The use of a delta-wing configuration offers several advantages for long-range one-way attack drones. It simplifies manufacturing, reduces structural complexity, increases internal fuel volume, and provides stable aerodynamic performance during long-duration flights.
Chinese Technology Could Have Played a Role
While comparisons with the Shahed are inevitable, another possible influence may lie in China. Pakistan’s defence industrial base has become increasingly integrated with Chinese aerospace and missile technologies over the past two decades. Joint programmes such as the JF-17 fighter aircraft, armed drones, precision-guided munitions, and missile systems have demonstrated the depth of this cooperation.
Chinese companies have developed numerous unmanned aerial vehicles featuring efficient composite structures, satellite navigation systems, autonomous flight controls, and economical piston engines suitable for long-endurance operations. Although no evidence has emerged linking any specific Chinese company to the D-248, it would not be surprising if subsystems such as flight control computers, satellite navigation modules, communication equipment, composite manufacturing techniques, or propulsion technologies originated from Chinese suppliers.
Heavy Industries Taxila has traditionally specialised in armoured vehicle production rather than advanced unmanned aircraft. That raises further questions regarding whether other Pakistani organisations, foreign technology partners, or imported subsystems contributed to the programme.
Strategic Shift Towards Affordable Long-Range Strike Systems
The emergence of the D-248 also reflects a broader global trend. Recent conflicts have demonstrated that long-range loitering munitions can deliver strategic effects at a fraction of the cost of cruise missiles. Rather than relying exclusively on expensive precision-guided weapons, militaries are increasingly investing in expendable unmanned strike platforms capable of attacking infrastructure, logistics hubs, air defence sites, and command centres.
If Pakistan succeeds in producing the D-248 in significant numbers, it could provide the country with a relatively economical means of expanding its long-range strike options. Its ability to remain airborne for over 12 hours would also permit flexible mission planning, allowing operators to loiter near target areas before attacking at an optimal moment.
Questions Still Outnumber Answers
Despite the impressive brochure specifications, many critical details remain undisclosed. Pakistan has not identified the engine powering the aircraft, the type of navigation system employed, whether the drone relies solely on satellite guidance or incorporates terrain matching, or whether it includes electro-optical seekers for terminal guidance.
Similarly, there has been no publicly released information regarding successful flight trials, operational deployment, production numbers, or confirmed induction into Pakistan’s armed forces.
Without demonstrated testing, the published specifications should be viewed as manufacturer claims rather than independently verified performance. The claimed endurance and range also suggest a substantial internal fuel fraction, leaving limited space for heavier warheads unless the aircraft employs an exceptionally lightweight composite airframe. These engineering trade-offs will become clearer only if additional technical information emerges.
A New Regional Capability Worth Monitoring
Whether the D-248 ultimately meets its advertised performance or not, its public unveiling highlights Pakistan’s growing interest in indigenous or locally assembled long-range unmanned strike systems.
The platform combines characteristics associated with Iran’s Shahed loitering munitions while operating within a defence industrial ecosystem that relies heavily on Chinese technology across multiple sectors. This combination has naturally fuelled speculation regarding possible foreign technical assistance, even though no official evidence has yet confirmed such involvement.

articles.title: EtherealX Unveils FSCC Engine and Pegasus Specs: A No-Preburner, No-Heat-Shield Bet on Full Reusability
articles.text:
Bengaluru’s EtherealX has been quietly working on something that, on paper at least, sounds almost too clever to be real. The startup has now shared fresh technical details about its proprietary engine cycle and the Pegasus upper-stage engine that runs on it — and the specs make for interesting reading, whether you’re a propulsion nerd or just watching India’s private space scene heat up.
Let’s talk numbers first. Pegasus is rated at 80 kN of thrust, with a chamber pressure of 100 bar and a vacuum specific impulse of 323 seconds. It runs on RP-1 and liquid oxygen — the same propellant combo that powered the Saturn V’s mighty F-1, though obviously at a very different scale. EtherealX is claiming combustion efficiency north of 99%, which, if it holds up during actual hot-fire testing, would be genuinely impressive. For context, most well-designed liquid rocket engines sit somewhere in the 96–98% range.
But here’s where things get unusual. Pegasus has no preburner.
If you follow rocket engines, you’ll know that staged combustion cycles — like SpaceX’s Raptor or the Russian RD-180 — route a portion of propellant through a separate preburner to generate hot gas that drives the turbopump. It’s powerful but complex, and it means dealing with extremely hot, oxygen-rich or fuel-rich gas running through your turbine blades. EtherealX has thrown that approach out entirely. Their Full Flow Segregated Cooling Cycle, or FSCC, does away with the preburner and instead leans on regenerative cooling — running both propellants through channels in the engine walls to absorb heat. That absorbed thermal energy is enough to vaporize and pressurize the RP-1/LOX before it hits the injector, which is essentially how an expander cycle work.
What makes this notable is that nobody has really made an expander-cycle engine work with RP-1/LOX before. Hydrogen is the usual coolant of choice for expander cycles because it absorbs heat beautifully and stays chemically stable. Kerosene is a different animal — it tends to crack and leave deposits when heated, which is one reason expander cycles have stayed in the hydrolox world. If EtherealX has genuinely solved that problem, it’s a meaningful engineering first: the world’s first RP-1/LOX thrust chamber assembly running on an expander-type cycle.
The turbopump, incidentally, is additively manufactured in-house, which keeps things compact and reduces part count
technologyNow for the part that raises the most eyebrows. EtherealX says its upper stage will come back through the atmosphere without any heat shield. Not a reduced one — none at all.
Every other company trying to recover an upper stage treats re-entry heat as the enemy. SpaceX’s Starship uses ceramic tiles. Blue Origin’s New Glenn plans ablative shielding. Stoke Space, probably the closest comparable effort globally, has its own active cooling approach. EtherealX’s idea is to route the re-entry plasma heat through the engine’s cooling channels and use that energy to drive the turbopump for a propulsive braking burn on the way down. As CEO Manu J. Nair puts it: “Why fight the re-entry heat when we can utilize it?”,.
The logic is that every kilogram of thermal protection you don’t carry is a kilogram of payload you can sell. But it’s also a claim that only really gets tested under actual orbital re-entry conditions, at velocities around 7.8 km/s. That’s why the company is deliberately skipping suborbital hop tests — anything slower won’t produce the thermal conditions the system is designed for, so there’s no point gathering data that doesn’t reflect reality
founderthesis
Before any of that happens, though, the engines need to prove themselves on the test stand. EtherealX plans to hot-fire both Pegasus and its larger 1.2 MN Stallion booster engine at Base 001, the company’s test facility in Cuddalore, Tamil Nadu, followed by clustered multi-engine firings. The company has indicated it will test multiple engine cycles during this campaign, not just FSCC, to map out performance margins and characterize how the hardware behaves under different operating modes
technology
All of this feeds into the Razor Crest Mk-1, a 71-metre medium-lift vehicle that’s meant to recover both stages — booster and upper stage — something no operational rocket anywhere currently does. SpaceX’s Falcon 9 only brings back the first stage and throws away the upper stage every single flight. EtherealX is betting that it can do what others have found too hard
officechai
The funding suggests investors are buying the thesis. The company has raised $26.3 million across four rounds, most recently a $20.5 million Series A that pushed its valuation to $80.5 million. More tellingly, it has secured $130 million in signed launch contracts from customers including Japan’s SpaceBD and Taiwan’s space agency TASA — all before the rocket has flown once
founderthesis.
None of this means the approach will work. Regenerative cooling with kerosene is notoriously finicky. Re-entering without a heat shield is unproven at the scale and velocities involved. And the gap between a compelling thermodynamic concept and flight-qualified hardware is enormous, measured in years and millions of dollars. But the next 18 months of testing at Tamil Nadu and the new 150-acre campus in Andhra Pradesh will tell us something real. Either FSCC is a genuine breakthrough in engine architecture, or it’s an ambitious idea that the fire hasn’t yet validated. Either way, it’s worth watching.

articles.text:
On August 18 and 19, 2026, two Turkish Air Force A400M transports touched down at PAF Base Murid in Pakistan’s Chakwal district. The aircraft — a single Airbus A400M-180, serial 18-0093, flying under callsign TUAF526 — made back-to-back sorties from Istanbul, routed through Afghanistan, and landed at a base that happens to be Pakistan’s primary hub for UAV and surveillance-strike operations
The cargo, according to OSINT analyst Abhinav (@ThatArticleGuy on X), was a massive shipment of Asisguard Songar armed drones — 850 of them, delivered in two batches
What the flight data shows
The attached flight-tracking table tells a clear story. On August 18, the Turkish A400M (Mode-S transponder 4B8213) flew Istanbul → Afghanistan → Pakistan, landing at Murid. The same aircraft was back in Pakistani airspace the next day, August 19, operating over Pakistan again Alongside the Turkish flights, Chinese Y-20 heavy military transports were tracked arriving at PAF Base Nur Khan in Rawalpindi and PAF Base Masroor in Karachi around the same window
This wasn’t a routine visit. Between roughly August 18 and 21, a concentrated 60-hour airlift saw dozens of Turkish C-130s and A400Ms, supplemented by Chinese military transports, landing at three Pakistani bases — Nur Khan, Masroor, and Murid. The scale and timing pointed to emergency resupply, not a standard military exchange ].
Why Murid matters
PAF Base Murid isn’t just any airbase. Located in Chakwal district of Punjab, it’s specialised as Pakistan’s operational centre for unmanned combat aerial vehicles, including Bayraktar platforms. Critically, Murid was among the key military installations struck by Indian precision munitions — including BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles — during Operation Sindoor in May 2025 .
Sending Turkish heavy transports loaded with drone-related cargo directly to a base that India had recently bombed sends a message: Pakistan isn’t just reconstituting — it’s rebuilding at the exact nodes that were hit.
The cargo: 850 Songar drones
According to the OSINT thread, the two A400M sorties carried a total of 850 Asisguard Songar armed drones, split as follows [cite:ac6b96e5]:
- 400× Songar MG GL — the machine gun + 40mm grenade launcher variant
- 400× Songar MG — the standard automatic machine gun version
- 50× Songar Togan — integrated with TÜBİTAK SAGE’s 81mm air-dropped mortar munition
These are all real, documented variants in Asisguard’s product line. The Songar MG carries a 5.56×45mm NATO assault rifle with 200 rounds, featuring an automatic gun stabiliser (OASIS) and recoil damping. The MG GL adds a 40mm grenade launcher with an effective range of 400–450 metres. The Togan variant is the heaviest hitter — an air-launched 81mm mortar with a circular error probable (CEP) of just 10 metres and a lethal blast radius of 35 metres
This isn’t Pakistan’s first encounter with Songar. During Operation Sindoor in May 2025, Pakistan launched 300–400 Songar drones across 36 locations from Leh to Sir Creek, targeting Indian military installations. Indian forces shot down many of them using kinetic and non-kinetic means, and forensic examination of the debris confirmed they were Turkish-made Asisguard Songar models. So the August deliveries represent a replenishment — and a significant upscale — of a drone fleet Pakistan had already used in combat against India.
What the Songar actually is
For context, the Songar is Turkey’s first indigenous armed drone system, developed by Ankara-based Asisguard and entering Turkish Armed Forces service in February 2020. It’s a quadrotor (technically an octocopter in a quadcopter configuration — eight carbon-fibre propellers), designed for tactical, low-altitude operations in day or night conditions [cite:97542873],[cite:012d91c6].
Key specs: maximum takeoff weight of 45 kg, payload capacity of about 9 kg, rotor-to-rotor span of 140–145 cm, flight time of up to 25 minutes, service ceiling of 3,000 metres above mean sea level, and an operational range of 3 km standard (extendable to 5–10 km with optional equipment). It uses both GPS and GLONASS navigation, supports autonomous and manual flight modes, and includes return-to-home functionality on link loss or low battery .
In short, these are short-range, infantry-deployable armed drones — not strategic strike platforms. But 850 of them, especially the mortar-equipped Togan variant, give Pakistan a substantial tactical drone swarm capability that can be deployed along the border or in counterinsurgency operations.
The bigger picture: Mecca Defence Pact and post-Sindoor resupply
The airlift didn’t happen in a vacuum. On August 7, 2026 — less than two weeks before the Turkish flights — Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, creating a collective security framework that binds Turkish military technology, Saudi financial resources, and Pakistani military manpower into a formal alliance .
Reporting indicates that during the Mecca agreement discussions, Pakistan’s Army Chief Asim Munir personally requested drones from Turkish President Erdogan, citing the heavy losses Pakistan’s drone fleet and air defence systems suffered during Operation Sindoor [cite:44cafe30]. Pakistan had received sufficient J-series fighter jets from China, but a large portion of its drones were destroyed in the May 2025 conflict .
Additional reporting suggests the Turkish cargo wasn’t limited to Songars — it may have also included Baykar Yiha-3 (K2) loitering munitions, Bayraktar TB2 drones with SATCOM terminals, Kemanke AI-guided cruise missiles, and even F-16 upgrade kits . The drone consignment was reportedly flown in under cover of darkness to evade satellite tracking, and stored at military facilities in Bahawalpur and Rawalpindi .
What’s confirmed and what isn’t
Here’s the honest breakdown. The flight data is solid and well-tracked across multiple OSINT platforms — the Turkish A400M flights to Murid, the Chinese Y-20s to Nur Khan and Masroor, the timing, the callsigns, all check out . The interpretation that this was drone-related resupply is shared across multiple defence analysis outlets .
However, neither the Turkish Ministry of National Defence nor Pakistan’s ISPR has released an official cargo manifest ]. The specific figure of 850 Songar drones, broken down into 400 MG GL + 400 MG + 50 Togan, appears to originate from the OSINT account’s analysis. The variant names are genuine, Pakistan’s prior use of Songar is confirmed, and the scale of resupply is consistent with reported losses — but the precise count should be treated as a well-reasoned OSINT estimate rather than verified fact.
What’s clear is that Pakistan is rapidly rebuilding its drone fleet at a base India recently struck, using Turkish hardware acquired under a new trilateral defence pact, and doing it quickly enough that 850 armed drones arrived within a single week. For anyone watching the India-Pakistan air balance, that’s the signal worth tracking.

articles.title: Operation Sindoor marked significant shift in India’s approach towards Pak: ex-Army chief Naravane
articles.text:
Operation Sindoor marked a “very significant shift” in India’s approach towards Pakistan as the strikes targeted not only terrorist hideouts near the border but also their supporters deep inside the neighbouring country, former Army chief General M M Naravane said on Saturday.
Speaking to reporters after attending a private event in Vadodara to promote the start-up ecosystem, he said the operation, carried out following the Pahalgam terror attack a year ago, demonstrated that those providing support to terrorists could not escape Indian action regardless of where they were located.
“Operation Sindoor, which took place after the Pahalgam attack, was a very necessary action,” said Naravane, who had served as the 28th Chief of the Army Staff.
Earlier, India’s military response had largely been focused on terrorist hideouts located close to the border, he said, referring to earlier terror attacks, including in Uri and Pulwama.
“Previously, whenever such attacks occurred — like after Uri, and Balakot strikes after Pulwama — we were mostly targeting terrorist hideouts close to the border.
“But this time, the strikes carried out targeted their supporters and those who provide them backing, wherever they may be — not just near the Line of Control, but deep inside Pakistan, in Muridke and Bahawalpur, from where they receive this support,” said general Naravane (retd).
He said India demonstrated that those providing support to terrorism “anywhere cannot escape”.
“As our Defence Minister Rajnath Singh had said, ‘we will enter their territory and eliminate them’, and there will be no protection for them. So, this was a very significant shift in our modus operandi,” the former Army chief said.
Asked about reports that Pakistan had become more active in the Sir Creek sector and was carrying out “Operation Ababil”, general Naravane (retd) said such activities happen, adding that he did not have complete information about the reported operation.
“These kinds of activities keep happening. I don’t have complete information about this right now since I am retired,” he said.
However, Indian armed forces remained vigilant and would take appropriate action if required, he added.
“I would like to say that whatever activity takes place, our forces always keep a close watch on it. There is nothing to panic about, and whatever action needs to be taken, appropriate action will be taken at the right time,” the former Army chief said.
Asked whether Pakistan was capable of taking on India, the former general said, “In my opinion, no.” On India-China relations, general Naravane (retd) said the recent talks between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi should be viewed in the context of the long-standing boundary dispute between the two countries.
He said the meeting was the 25th round of Special Representative-level talks and was not taking place for the first time.
“This discussion that took place — the 25th round of Special Representative-level talks between Ajit Doval from our side and Foreign Minister Wang Yi from China — is not happening for the first time,” he added.
He said the key point to keep in mind is that there is a boundary dispute between India and China.
“Exactly where the boundary lies has not been clearly demarcated either on maps or on the ground. It is because of this lack of demarcation that occasional disputes arise between India and China,” the former Army chief added.
On the proposed theatre commands, General Naravane (retd) said the discussion on theatreisation of the armed forces had begun after the Kargil War and that it was not a new concept.
“The discussion on theaterisation first began after the Kargil War. It has already been 25 to 26 years since then. Theaterisation is not a new concept; it is a continuous process and an evolution,” he said.
The former Army chief further said there was broad agreement to establish theatre commands in India in view of rapidly changing modern warfare and shorter decision-making cycles.
Everyone agrees that such theatre commands should be established in India as well, he said.
“Considering the way the nature of modern warfare is transforming and decision cycles are becoming progressively shorter, it is essential that we move toward theaterisation as expeditiously as possible,” the former Army chief said.

articles.title: Javelin anti-tank system necessary to thwart any coordinated attack on India: Ex military personnel
articles.text:
India’s purchase of the Javelin anti-tank system from the US was “necessary to thwart any possible coordinated attack from Pakistan or China” in the future, given these two countries’ tank capabilities, former military personnel said on Friday.
The responses came after US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor confirmed the deal.
In a post on X, Gor said: “In a BIG news! India plans to buy the battle-tested Javelin anti-tank system. Just as @secwar (Pete Hegseth) highlighted at the May 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, this is a great step forward in the U.S.-India defense relationship and opens the door to co-production possibilities. The engagement between our two nations is at record high levels!”
Speaking to IANS, defence expert Major General P.K. Sehgal (Retd.) said: “First of all, India clearly understands that Pakistan and China can launch a coordinated attack. Both possess substantial tank capabilities. Currently, India faces a significant deficiency in anti-tank guided missiles. To address this deficiency, India had been trying for a considerable time to acquire the Javelin anti-tank weapon system from the United States, but there had been no forward movement.”
“Now, Gor’s statements clearly indicate that forward movement is taking place and a political decision has been reached, which means these anti-tank missiles could arrive in India soon,” he added.
Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (retd) noted that “tank battles are common” in modern warfare, citing the Russia-Ukraine war as an example.
“India’s border is very vast; Pakistan, Bangladesh, China and tank battles have become very common. We have seen it in Ukraine, in Iraq, in the 1971 war, in 1965, Khemkaran, etc…all these are remembered,” he told IANS.
“So, in these tank battles, when an enemy tank comes, you destroy it either with a tank, a tank gun, or with anti-tank weapons; an anti-tank guided missile is very effective…so we have signed this deal with America,” he said.
With the signing of a Letter of Offer and Acceptance (LOA) between India and the US, the former becomes a customer of the Javelin system, an advanced, medium-range, fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile.
The Javelin is used by the US Army, US Marine Corps, and numerous international customers and is designed for use against a wide array of targets, including armoured vehicles and fortified positions. The equipment is a man-portable anti-tank missile system jointly developed by Lockheed Martin and RTX for use against armoured targets.
